1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. IAM: Identity and Access Management; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; SCP: service control policy; VPC: Virtual Private Cloud; MFA: multi-factor authentication; RDS: Relational Database Service; KMS: Key Management Service; ECS: Elastic Container Service; LF: Lake Formation; SAML: Security Assertion Markup Language; ACL: access control list

  • Create custom IAM policies when a managed policy does not meet the needs
  • Store application and database credentials in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store
  • Give database users, groups and roles access in Amazon Redshift
  • Manage permissions through AWS Lake Formation for Redshift, EMR, Athena and S3
  • Choose role-based, tag-based and attribute-based authorization
  • Write policies that follow least privilege

Authentication (Module 14) proves who; authorization decides what that identity may do with which data.

2Custom IAM Policies (skills 4.2.1 and 4.2.6)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Draws the Lines

  • Dispatchers may read live truck data, never invoices
  • Finance may read invoices but not customer phone numbers
  • EU analysts may see only EU customers' rows
  • Your job: grant exactly what each group needs and nothing more
Policy type Use
AWS managed policy Created and updated by AWS for common jobs (for example AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess): quick, but often too broad
Customer managed policy Your own reusable policy: versioned, attachable to many identities: the right choice when a managed policy does not fit
Inline policy Embedded in one identity: for a strict one-to-one relationship
Resource-based policy Attached to the resource (bucket, key, queue, secret) with a Principal
Permissions boundary / SCP Maximums that grant nothing on their own

Policy structure

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::kestrel-curated", "arn:aws:s3:::kestrel-curated/telemetry/*"],
    "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/team": "dispatch" } }
  }]
}
  • Effect (Allow or Deny), Action (API calls), Resource (ARNs), Condition (optional rules), Principal (only in resource-based policies)
  • Evaluation: everything is denied by default; an explicit Deny always wins; otherwise an Allow is needed (and SCPs and boundaries must also allow)

Building least privilege (skill 4.2.6)

  • Start from nothing, add the specific actions and resources the job needs (name the bucket and prefix, not *); avoid "Action": "*" and "Resource": "*"
  • Use conditions: source VPC endpoint, MFA present, secure transport only, tags, organization ID, time
  • Find what is really used: IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail activity, validate policies (warnings, errors) and report unused access; last accessed information shows unused permissions to remove
  • Test with the IAM policy simulator; review regularly; split broad roles by job (one role per pipeline)
  • Use guardrails: SCPs and permissions boundaries cap what administrators can grant
Exam tip

"A managed policy gives too much access" → write a customer managed policy with only the needed actions on specific resources, and use Access Analyzer to generate it from activity.

3Storing Application and Database Credentials (skill 4.2.2)

AWS Secrets Manager AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
Purpose Secrets (database credentials, API keys) Configuration values and secrets
Rotation Built-in automatic rotation (managed for RDS, Aurora, Redshift; Lambda for others) None built in
Encryption KMS, always SecureString uses KMS; plain String is not encrypted
Structure Secrets with versions and staging labels Hierarchies (/kestrel/prod/db/host), tiers (standard and advanced)
Cost Charged per secret and API call Standard parameters are free; advanced tier has a charge
Cross-account Resource policy Limited (advanced tier sharing)
Pick it when Credentials must rotate Plain configuration or secrets that do not need rotation at low cost
  • Access with IAM: the job's role gets secretsmanager:GetSecretValue (and KMS decrypt on the key) for that one secret; never put credentials in code, environment variables in clear text, job parameters or logs
  • Glue connections, Lambda, ECS, EMR and Redshift can reference a secret
Exam tip

"Store database credentials that rotate automatically" → Secrets Manager. "Store non-secret configuration cheaply" → Parameter Store.

4Database Authorization in Amazon Redshift (skill 4.2.3)

  • Authentication can be database users and passwords, IAM (temporary credentials), or federated identities (IAM Identity Center and identity providers)
  • Authorization inside the database uses users, groups and roles:
    • Users and groups collect permissions; roles (role-based access control) are named sets of permissions that can be granted to users and other roles; superuser bypasses checks (avoid)
    • GRANT and REVOKE on schemas, tables, views, functions and procedures, down to columns; default privileges apply to future objects
  • Finer controls:
    • Column-level grants for sensitive columns
    • Row-level security (RLS) policies filter rows by user or role (for example a region)
    • Dynamic data masking (DDM) hides or partly shows values (for example last four digits) by role without changing the data
  • Lake and external data: Redshift Spectrum and data sharing also use Lake Formation or IAM (below)
CREATE ROLE finance_analyst;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE invoices TO ROLE finance_analyst;
GRANT ROLE finance_analyst TO analyst_amy;
Exam tip

"Analysts must see only some columns of a Redshift table" → column-level GRANT (or a view, or dynamic data masking). "Show only their region's rows" → row-level security.

5Permissions through AWS Lake Formation (skill 4.2.4)

  • AWS Lake Formation is a central place to grant and revoke access to data lake data in S3 and tables in the Glue Data Catalog, instead of managing S3 bucket policies and IAM per user
  • What you can grant: database, table, column permissions (SELECT, INSERT, DESCRIBE, ALTER, DROP), data location permissions (where new tables may point), and grant option
  • Fine-grained controls:
    • Column-level security: include or exclude columns
    • Row-level and cell-level security: data filters with a row filter expression and column list
    • LF-tags (tag-based access control): tag databases, tables and columns (sensitivity=pii, domain=finance) and grant by tag; scales to thousands of tables
  • Principals: IAM users and roles, IAM Identity Center and SAML identities, other accounts
  • Works with: Amazon Athena, Redshift Spectrum, Amazon EMR, AWS Glue, Amazon QuickSight and others: the engine asks Lake Formation, which vends temporary credentials for only the allowed data
  • Cross-account sharing: grant to another account (using AWS RAM underneath); the recipient creates resource links in its own catalog
  • Turn it on: by default, catalog resources may be open to IAM (the IAMAllowedPrincipals group); to enforce Lake Formation permissions, revoke that default and register the S3 location with Lake Formation
  • Both layers must allow: IAM must permit the call, Lake Formation must permit the data
  • Auditing: CloudTrail logs Lake Formation grants and data access
Exam tip

"Different teams must see different columns and rows of the same lake tables, managed centrally" → AWS Lake Formation (data filters and LF-tags), not per-bucket policies.

6Role-Based, Tag-Based and Attribute-Based Authorization (skill 4.2.5)

Model How it decides Example Strength Watch for
Role-based (RBAC) Job function → role or group with a fixed permission set FinanceAnalyst role may read invoices Simple, easy to audit Role explosion as teams grow
Tag-based (TBAC) Resource tags drive access (LF-tags, resource tags in policies) Anyone with domain=finance permission can read tables tagged domain=finance Scales with data; new tagged tables inherit access Tag governance: who may tag?
Attribute-based (ABAC) Compare attributes of the principal and the resource and context Allow if aws:PrincipalTag/team equals aws:ResourceTag/team One policy for many teams; fewer policies Consistent tags are essential
  • Policy-based is the general idea: permissions come from policies attached to identities or resources
  • Combine them: roles for broad job functions, tags and attributes for fine, scalable control
  • Protect the tags: restrict who may create or change the tags that drive access
Exam tip

"Avoid creating a new policy for every team" → ABAC with matching principal and resource tags. "Grant by data domain or sensitivity across the lake" → Lake Formation LF-tags.

7Exam Q&A

7.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Finance analysts must query a Redshift table but must not see the card_number column. What is the simplest approach?

  • AGive the analysts superuser access so that they can choose columns
  • BGrant SELECT on only the permitted columns, or apply dynamic data masking to the column
  • CCopy the table to S3 without the column every night by a script
  • DRemove the table and let the analysts use a spreadsheet instead
Show the answer

Answer: B. Redshift supports column-level GRANT and dynamic data masking to hide sensitive columns by role.

S2Several teams query the same S3 data lake tables with Athena and Redshift Spectrum. Each team may see only certain columns and rows, and the company wants central management. Which service should be used?

  • AOne S3 bucket policy for each user who queries the lake
  • BAWS Config rules that flag the tables that are too open
  • CAmazon Macie jobs that classify the objects in the buckets
  • DAWS Lake Formation with data filters and LF-tags
Show the answer

Answer: D. Lake Formation centralizes permissions on catalog tables, columns and rows for engines such as Athena and Redshift Spectrum.

S3An organization has dozens of teams and wants one IAM policy that lets each team access only resources tagged with its own team name. Which approach fits?

  • AAttribute-based access control comparing aws:PrincipalTag/team with aws:ResourceTag/team
  • BRole-based access control with one separate role for each team and each resource, plus a policy for each
  • CNetwork ACLs on the subnets that hold the data stores
  • DResource-based policies written on every single object
Show the answer

Answer: A. ABAC compares attributes of the principal and the resource, so one policy covers many teams.

S4Which TWO actions help create least-privilege policies? (Select TWO.)

  • AUse IAM Access Analyzer to generate a policy from CloudTrail activity
  • BGrant "Action": "" on "Resource": "" and monitor
  • CShare one administrator role among all pipelines
  • DReview last accessed information and remove unused permissions
  • EDisable the policy simulator
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. Access Analyzer can build policies from actual usage, and last accessed information shows permissions that can be removed. Wildcard and shared admin permissions break least privilege.

8Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Policy types AWS managed (broad), customer managed (own, versioned, reusable), inline, resource-based, boundaries/SCPs (maximums)
Evaluation Default deny, explicit deny wins, otherwise an allow is required (and SCP/boundary must allow)
Least privilege Specific actions and ARNs, conditions, Access Analyzer (generate from CloudTrail, validate, unused access), last accessed, policy simulator
Credentials Secrets Manager (rotation, per-secret charge) vs Parameter Store (config, free standard tier, SecureString, no rotation)
Redshift Users, groups, roles (RBAC), GRANT/REVOKE to column level, row-level security, dynamic data masking, avoid superuser
Lake Formation Central grants on databases, tables, columns, rows (data filters), LF-tags, S3 data locations; works with Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, Glue, QuickSight; cross-account via RAM; turn off IAM-only default
RBAC / TBAC / ABAC Roles by job; resource tags; compare principal and resource attributes (one policy, many teams)
